caption:
Outside researchers at METR spent 11 weeks reviewing Anthropic's internal data and interviewing its staff.
They estimate Anthropic is improving its AI on well-specified tasks about twice as fast as a year ago, mostly because AI is helping build AI.
Anthropic's own CEO asked the industry to slow down in September.

Should AI labs let AI speed up their own research?

paragraphs.text: Anthropic is improving the capabilities of its AI models on well-specified tasks about twice as fast as it was a year earlier, according to an independent assessment released on November 5, 2026, by METR, a nonprofit based in Berkeley, California, that evaluates AI systems. The Associated Press reported that the group attributed much of the speedup to AI helping to improve AI.

METR reviewed about 11 weeks of Anthropic's internal data, from mid-August through late October 2026, and interviewed employees. Anthropic invited the review ahead of its planned stock market debut, the AP reported. According to Unite.AI, the work ran from August 12 to October 29 with the equivalent of 2.5 full-time staff and roughly 15 staff interviews, and Dataconomy reported that METR researchers worked at Anthropic's San Francisco headquarters during that period.

METR concluded that Anthropic made as much progress on benchmarks in the past year as it did from October 2023 to October 2025, Dataconomy reported. Using Anthropic's internal benchmark index, the group estimated that scores have grown 1.9 times faster since October 2025, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 1.5 to 2.8 times, according to Unite.AI.

The group said it could confidently rule out growth in training compute as the cause, and its best explanation was AI assistance in Anthropic's own research. It also said it did not observe bottlenecks in computing power or data that would stop the acceleration over the next year, while warning that it may have missed some constraints.

Anthropic also shared informal internal Slack polls. In them, staff reported an average productivity increase of about 12 times from the company's most capable internal model as of October 2026. METR described the polls as weak evidence that may not represent employees broadly.

METR said AI is not yet able to make highly significant, fully autonomous contributions to Anthropic's research, but it described early signs that such contributions could grow soon, according to the AP and Dataconomy.

Anthropic's redactions limited how much METR could publish, and the group said they removed much of the evidence it found most informative, including detailed forecasts. Anthropic said the redactions protect confidential information that could help other developers, Unite.AI reported. METR also noted internal disagreement and uncertainty about its estimate.

The group cautioned that the acceleration may apply only to well-specified tasks that can be graded automatically rather than messy real-world work, or that Anthropic may have understated its earlier progress. It also said a public risk report Anthropic published in August understated the acceleration that was taking place. METR is funded by donations and does not accept payment for its work, though the companies it evaluates provide access and free tokens, the AP reported.

The findings come after Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei wrote in a September 12 essay that the industry should slow the pace at which it improves AI capabilities, warning that AI building the next generation of AI could outrun the ability to understand and control these systems. METR's assessment period overlapped with that call. Anthropic did not immediately respond to the AP's request for comment. The company plans to go public later in November, in what could be the largest stock offering ever, according to the AP.

The report is one of the first outside attempts to measure how much AI is speeding up a frontier lab's own work, and it arrives as Anthropic asks public investors to back it. Because much of the strongest evidence was redacted, readers have to rely on METR's judgment rather than the data itself, which limits how much weight the roughly twofold figure can carry.
Watch whether Anthropic publishes more of the underlying data or its own response to METR before its planned IPO, and whether other AI labs agree to similar outside reviews of their research pace.
